Ensemble Model for Glioma Tumor Classification using TCGA Data

DA5030

Pradhan, Dinesh

Spring 2026

Introduction

This project builds an ensemble classification model to predict Glioma tumor grade (GBM vs LGG) using genomic and clinical data from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) program. The goal is to classify tumors as either Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) or Lower Grade Glioma (LGG) based on gene mutation profiles, demographic features, and clinical variables.

Data Source

The dataset is sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository — TCGA-LGG and TCGA-GBM dataset. It contains 862 observations and 27 variables including 20 gene mutation features (IDH1, TP53, ATRX, etc.), clinical features (Age, Gender, Race), and the target variable Grade (GBM or LGG).

Approach of the project

The modeling approach follows the CRISP-DM framework — data understanding, preparation, modeling, and evaluation. Three base models are trained (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, C5.0) each with hyperparameter tuning and bagging, and combined into a heterogeneous ensemble for final prediction.

Load Library

I use the library function from the R was used to load the library. THis is important as it will help us to use the function in the library. The ggplot2 was used for the visualization, the vIM was used for the KNN model, the car was used for the VIF to check the multicolonearity, the caret library was used to stratified splitting of the data, the randomfroest library was used for the random forest model, the C50 library was used for the C50 model.

Exploring the data

Checking the target column

# Checking the distribution of the target varible
table(df$Grade)
## 
## GBM LGG 
## 363 499
prop.table(table(df$Grade))
## 
##       GBM       LGG 
## 0.4211137 0.5788863

I examined the distribution of the target variable Grade using frequency counts and proportions to understand the class balance in the dataset by applying table(df$Grade) and prop.table(table(df$Grade)). This step is important because knowing whether the dataset is balanced or imbalanced directly affects model performance and the choice of evaluation metrics. The results show that there are 363 GBM observations and 499 LGG observations, with proportions of 0.421 for GBM and 0.579 for LGG, indicating a moderate class imbalance where LGG is the majority class. This is necessary to identify potential bias toward the majority class and to justify the use of metrics like F1-score and techniques such as class weighting or threshold tuning in later stages of the modeling process.

The results show that no variables are purely numeric (0), while all features including Grade, Project, Case_ID and others are treated as categorical. This is necessary because it informs preprocessing decisions such as encoding for models like logistic regression, while models like Random Forest can handle categorical variables directly.

Converting the age to numeric

I converted the Age_at_diagnosis column into a numeric variable by extracting the numeric age using sub() and storing it in a new variable Age_years, followed by removing the original column. This was done because the age information was stored as text and needed to be converted into a numeric format for proper use in modeling algorithms. The transformation successfully created a usable numeric feature (14 to 89), replacing the non-numeric representation. This step is necessary because machine learning models require numeric inputs for meaningful computation and to ensure accurate model performance.

This is necessary because identifying missing values helps decide appropriate handling strategies such as imputation or removal to ensure the model is trained on complete and reliable data.

Target distribution (Class imbalance)

I visualized the distribution of the target variable Grade using a bar plot created with ggplot2 to better understand the class balance in the dataset. This was done because visual representation provides a clearer and more intuitive understanding of how the classes are distributed compared to numerical summaries alone. The plot shows that the LGG class has a higher count than the GBM class, confirming a moderate class imbalance in the dataset. I chose to keep the class imbalance as it is and did not apply techniques like oversampling or undersampling because the imbalance is not severe and models like Random Forest are relatively robust to such imbalance. Additionally, altering the class distribution could distort the original data characteristics. This is necessary because acknowledging and consciously handling (or not handling) class imbalance ensures transparency in modeling decisions and supports the use of appropriate evaluation metrics like F1-score.

Clinical features column distribution

I visualized the distribution of key clinical categorical features (Gender, Race, and Primary Diagnosis) to understand their data spread and category representation. This was done to identify any imbalance or dominance of certain categories, which could influence model learning. The plots show that Male is the dominant gender, white is the most frequent race, and Glioblastoma appears most commonly among diagnoses, indicating uneven distributions across categories. This is necessary to understand feature characteristics, detect potential bias, and guide preprocessing or modeling decisions if required.

Gene mutation distribution

I analyzed the distribution of key gene mutations (IDH1, TP53, ATRX, EGFR, and PTEN) to understand how frequently mutations occur across the dataset. This was done to identify whether mutation patterns are balanced or skewed, which can influence model learning. The observations show that most genes have a higher number of non-mutated cases compared to mutated ones, indicating an imbalance in mutation presence. I chose not to apply any balancing techniques because these mutation patterns reflect the true biological distribution of the data, and altering them could distort meaningful relationships. Additionally, models like Random Forest can handle such imbalance effectively without requiring explicit adjustments. This is necessary to preserve the original data characteristics while still allowing the model to learn important patterns.

Imputation of the missing value (Using the KNN model)

# Checking the missing value
sum(is.na(df_clean))
## [1] 5
# Applying the KNN imputation
df_imputed <- kNN(df_clean, k = 5)

# Removing the extra column
df_imputed <- df_imputed[, !grepl("_imp", names(df_imputed))]

# Back checking any missing value
sum(is.na(df_imputed))
## [1] 0

I handled missing values in the dataset using KNN imputation with k = 5 to estimate and replace missing entries based on similar observations. This was done to preserve the dataset size and avoid losing information that could occur if rows were removed. Initially, there were 5 missing values, and after imputation, all missing values were successfully removed (0). This is necessary because most machine learning algorithms cannot handle missing data directly, and proper imputation ensures the dataset is complete and suitable for modeling while maintaining underlying data patterns.

Corelation and associate analysis

chi square test

I performed a Chi-Square test to evaluate the association between each gene mutation and the target variable Grade. This was done to identify which features have a statistically significant relationship with tumor classification. The results show that several genes such as IDH1, ATRX, PTEN, and EGFR have very low p-values, indicating a strong association with the target variable, while some genes like BCOR, PIK3CA, and FAT4 have high p-values, suggesting little to no significant relationship. This is necessary for feature selection, as it helps in identifying important predictors that contribute to the model while potentially removing irrelevant features to improve performance and interpret.

Corelation age and Grade

##       cor

I performed a Pearson correlation test between Age_years and the target variable Grade (converted to numeric) to assess their relationship. This was done to understand whether age has a linear association with tumor classification. The results show a moderate positive correlation of 0.537 with a highly significant p-value (1.446739e-65), indicating that age is strongly associated with the tumor grade. This is necessary to identify important numerical features that contribute to the model and to support their inclusion in the predictive analysis.

I analyzed the correlation between gene mutations by converting them into binary format and computing a correlation matrix. This was done to identify relationships between different gene mutations and detect any multicollinearity. The results show that most correlations are relatively low, indicating weak relationships between genes, although some moderate positive correlations exist (e.g., between TP53 and ATRX, IDH1 and ATRX) and some negative correlations (e.g., IDH1 with PTEN and EGFR). Overall, there is no strong multicollinearity among features. This is necessary to ensure that the model is not affected by highly correlated predictors, which could reduce interpretability and stability of model.

I performed K-Means clustering on the mutation data (converted into binary format) to identify natural groupings of samples based on gene mutation patterns. This was done to explore whether mutation profiles can separate the data into meaningful clusters without using the target variable. The elbow method showed a gradual decrease in WSS, and I selected k = 2 for simplicity and interpretability. The clustering resulted in two nearly equal-sized groups (437 and 425). The cluster centers indicate distinct mutation patterns, where one cluster is characterized by high IDH1, TP53, and ATRX mutation rates, while the other shows higher PTEN and EGFR mutation presence. When compared with the actual tumor grades, the clusters align well, achieving an alignment of 85.4%, indicating strong separation between GBM and LGG based on mutation profiles. This is necessary to validate that the features capture meaningful biological structure and support their usefulness in classification modeling.

PCA

## [1] 14
## [1] 16

I performed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the mutation data to reduce dimensionality and understand how variance is distributed across features. This was done to identify the number of components required to capture most of the information in the dataset. The results show that the first few principal components explain a moderate portion of the variance, and approximately 14 components are required to capture 80% of the variance, while 16 components are needed to capture 90%. This indicates that the data is spread across multiple dimensions rather than being dominated by a few features. This is necessary to assess dimensionality, reduce redundancy, and understand the complexity of the dataset before modeling.

Top feature loadings for PC1

I examined the PCA loadings to identify which gene mutations contribute most to the principal components, particularly PC1. This was done to understand which features drive the major variation in the dataset. The results show that genes such as IDH1, ATRX, PTEN, EGFR, and TP53 have the highest absolute loadings on PC1, indicating they are the most influential in separating the data. Positive and negative loadings suggest opposite mutation patterns across samples. This is necessary because identifying key contributing features helps in understanding the biological significance of the data and supports feature importance interpretation in downstream modeling.

I prepared the dataset for Logistic Regression by applying one-hot encoding to convert categorical variables into numeric indicator variables and then added the target variable Grade back to the transformed dataset. This was done because Logistic Regression requires numeric input features and cannot directly handle categorical variables in their original form. After encoding, the dataset was expanded to 862 observations and 31 variables, where each category is represented in a machine-readable format suitable for model training. This is necessary to ensure that the Logistic Regression model can correctly process the data, estimate coefficients for each predictor, and make accurate classifications.

Normalization check

## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  df_log$Age_years
## W = 0.98279, p-value = 1.549e-08

I examined the distribution of the Age_years variable using a histogram and performed the Shapiro-Wilk test to assess normality. This was done to determine whether transformation is required before modeling. The histogram shows a reasonably symmetric distribution, and although the Shapiro-Wilk test gives a significant p-value (1.549047e-08), this is expected due to the large sample size, where even small deviations from normality become statistically significant. Therefore, I chose not to apply any transformation as the data is visually well distributed. Additionally, transformation is mainly important for models like Logistic Regression that assume linear relationships, while tree-based models such as Random Forest and C5.0 do not require normalization or distributional assumptions. This is necessary to avoid unnecessary preprocessing while ensuring model assumptions are appropriately considered.

Spliting the data train/test

## [1] 691  31
## [1] 171  31

I split the dataset into training and validation sets using an 80:20 ratio while maintaining the class distribution of the target variable. This was done to train the model on one portion of the data and evaluate its performance on unseen data. The training set contains 691 observations and the validation set contains 171 observations, with both having 31 features. This is necessary to assess the model’s generalization ability and ensure that it performs well on new, unseen data rather than just memorizing the training data.

Scaling the data

I standardized the numerical features in the dataset by centering and scaling them using the mean and standard deviation calculated from the training data. This was done to ensure that all features are on a similar scale, which is important for models like Logistic Regression that are sensitive to feature magnitude. The same scaling parameters from the training set were applied to the validation set to prevent data leakage. This is necessary to improve model convergence, ensure fair contribution of all features, and maintain consistency between training and validation data. Additionally, scaling is not required for tree-based models like Random Forest and C5.0, as they are not affected by feature scale.

Checking the multicolinearity using vif

I checked for multicollinearity among the features using Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to identify highly correlated predictors. This was done because high multicollinearity can negatively affect models like Logistic Regression by making coefficient estimates unstable. The results show that features such as Cluster2 and IDH1NOT_MUTATED have high VIF values (25.807 and 23.632), indicating strong multicollinearity. Despite this, I chose not to remove them at this stage because they may carry important predictive information and tree-based models are not affected by multicollinearity. This is necessary to understand feature relationships and make informed decisions about feature selection while balancing model performance and interpretability.

Data traning for Random forest model

Spliting the data train/test Random Forest

I split the dataset into training and validation sets for the Random Forest model using an 80:20 ratio while preserving the class distribution. This was done to train the model on one portion of the data and evaluate its performance on unseen data. The training set contains 691 observations and the validation set contains 171 observations. This is necessary to ensure that the model generalizes well and does not overfit the training data.

Data traning for C50 model

## [1] 171  25

This was done to ensure that the model is trained on one portion of the data and evaluated on unseen data for fair performance assessment. The training set contains 691 observations and the validation set contains 171 observations, with 25 features. This is necessary to evaluate the model’s ability to generalize and prevent overfitting.

I trained an ensemble of five Logistic Regression models by repeatedly sampling different subsets from the training data and assigning higher class weights to the GBM cases to reduce the effect of class imbalance. This was done to improve model stability, reduce variance from a single training split, and make the model more sensitive to the minority class. The predicted probabilities from all five models were then averaged to obtain a final ensemble probability for validation. The model summaries show that variables such as TP53, IDH2, Age_years, and Cluster2 were repeatedly important across multiple models, while a few coefficients were not estimated because of singularities caused by redundant encoded categories. Overall, the residual deviance was much lower than the null deviance across models, indicating that the fitted models explained the target better than the intercept-only model. This is necessary because Logistic Regression serves as an interpretable baseline model, and using an ensemble with class weighting improves robustness and classification performance on imbalanced data.

Tuning the threshold

I tuned the classification threshold for the Logistic Regression ensemble by evaluating F1-scores across multiple probability cutoffs ranging from 0.10 to 0.90. This was done because the default threshold (0.5) may not be optimal, especially in the presence of class imbalance. The results show that the best F1-score of 0.87 was achieved at a threshold of 0.5, indicating an optimal balance between precision and recall. This is necessary because optimizing the threshold improves classification performance and ensures that the model makes better predictions for both classes rather than relying on a fixed default cutoff.

C50 Model traning

Tuning the c50 boosting trials

## [1] 5

I tuned the boosting parameter (trials) of the C5.0 model by evaluating multiple values to determine the optimal number of boosting iterations. This was done to improve model performance, as boosting helps combine multiple weak learners to form a stronger model. The results show that the best performance was achieved at trials = 5, with the highest F1-score of 0.865 and strong accuracy. Increasing trials beyond this point did not improve performance and even led to slight degradation, indicating potential overfitting. This is necessary because tuning the boosting parameter helps find the right balance between model complexity and generalization performance.

Training C5.0 bagging model

I trained an ensemble of five C5.0 models by creating bootstrap samples (sampling with replacement) from the training dataset and using the optimal number of boosting trials for each model. This was done to improve model stability and reduce variance by combining multiple models trained on slightly different data. Each model learns different patterns, and combining them helps achieve more robust predictions. This is necessary because ensemble methods enhance generalization performance and reduce the risk of overfitting compared to relying on a single model.

The results show that the best F1-score of 0.874 was achieved at a threshold of 0.4, indicating the most effective decision boundary for classifying GBM cases. This is necessary because threshold tuning improves model performance and ensures better handling of class imbalance by optimizing prediction decisions.

This was done to leverage the strengths of each individual model, as different algorithms capture different patterns in the data. The resulting ensemble probabilities show a well-distributed range, indicating that the model is effectively capturing variation in prediction confidence. This step is necessary because ensemble models generally improve overall performance, reduce model-specific bias, and provide more robust and stable predictions compared to individual models.

Threshold Tuning for Ensemble

I tuned the classification threshold for the heterogeneous ensemble model by evaluating F1-scores across thresholds from 0.10 to 0.90. This was done to identify the optimal cutoff that balances precision and recall for GBM classification. The results show that the best F1-score of 0.863 is achieved at a threshold of 0.4, indicating the most effective decision boundary for the ensemble predictions. However, compared to individual models, the ensemble shows lower performance, suggesting that simple averaging may dilute strong signals from better-performing models. This step is necessary to ensure fair evaluation and to confirm whether combining models actually improves performance.

Ensemble Function

I created an ensemble prediction function to combine the predicted probabilities from Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and C5.0, calculate the average probability for the GBM class, and convert it into the final class prediction using the optimal ensemble threshold. This was done to make the ensemble process reusable, organized, and easy to apply to any new set of model probabilities. The output provides both the final probability for GBM and the corresponding predicted class for each observation, making the results more interpretable. This is necessary because defining a separate prediction function improves workflow clarity, ensures consistency in ensemble prediction, and allows the final model to be applied efficiently to validation or future unseen data.

Model Evaluation

K fold cross validation

I defined a 5-fold cross-validation strategy to evaluate model performance more reliably by repeatedly splitting the training data into different subsets. This was done to reduce dependence on a single train-validation split and obtain a more stable estimate of how the models perform on unseen data. In this setup, the data is divided into five folds, where four folds are used for training and one fold is used for validation in each iteration, and this process is repeated five times. I also enabled class probabilities, used a summary function suitable for two-class classification, and saved the final predictions from each fold for later evaluation. This is necessary because cross-validation provides a more robust assessment of model generalization, helps detect overfitting, and supports fair comparison across models.

Logistic regression k fold

I evaluated the Logistic Regression model using 5-fold cross-validation on the training data. This was done to obtain a more reliable estimate of model performance by assessing it across multiple validation folds rather than relying on a single split. The cross-validation results show an average ROC of 0.896, sensitivity of 0.907, and specificity of 0.838, indicating strong overall discrimination and balanced classification performance. The relatively small standard deviations across folds suggest that the model performs consistently. This is necessary because cross-validation provides a robust measure of generalization performance and helps confirm that the Logistic Regression model is stable and not overly dependent on one particular training split.

Random forest K fold

I evaluated the Random Forest model using 5-fold cross-validation with the optimal mtry value (4) identified during tuning. This was done to ensure that the model’s performance is consistent across different subsets of the training data. The cross-validation results show an average ROC of 0.9, sensitivity of 0.931, and specificity of 0.83, indicating strong classification performance with a good balance between detecting GBM and LGG cases. The relatively low standard deviations suggest stable model behavior across folds. This is necessary because cross-validation confirms that the Random Forest model generalizes well and is not overfitting to a specific training split.

C5.0 k FOld

I evaluated the C5.0 model using 5-fold cross-validation with the optimal number of boosting trials (5). This was done to assess the model’s consistency and generalization across different subsets of the training data. The results show an average ROC of 0.904, sensitivity of 0.9, and specificity of 0.83, indicating strong predictive performance with a good balance between correctly identifying GBM and LGG cases. The low variation across folds suggests stable model behavior. This is necessary because cross-validation ensures that the C5.0 model is robust, reliable, and not overfitting to a particular subset of the data.

Summary of the K fold result across all model

I summarized the 5-fold cross-validation results for all three models—Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and C5.0—to compare their overall performance. This was done to identify which model generalizes best based on ROC, sensitivity, and specificity. The results show that all three models perform similarly, with C5.0 achieving the highest ROC (0.9042), indicating slightly better discrimination ability. Logistic Regression shows the highest sensitivity (0.9072), meaning it is better at identifying GBM cases, while C5.0 provides a better balance between sensitivity and specificity. This comparison is necessary to select the most suitable model and understand the trade-offs between different approaches before finalizing the predictive model.

Comparision of model

I compared the final performance of all models—Logistic Regression, Random Forest, C5.0, and the Heterogeneous Ensemble—using key evaluation metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, and Kappa. This was done to identify the best-performing model and understand the trade-offs between them. The results show that Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and C5.0 all achieve similar accuracy (0.883), with Logistic Regression having slightly higher sensitivity, while Random Forest and C5.0 provide a better balance between sensitivity and specificity. In contrast, the heterogeneous ensemble performs worse across all metrics, indicating that simple averaging did not improve performance in this case. This comparison is necessary to make an informed decision about the final model, and based on the results, Random Forest or C5.0 can be considered more robust choices due to their balanced performance.
